Lumina Grand EC offers flexible homes and green, smart living with nods to quarry landscape
article:
Bukit Batok’s granite quarrying past provided the design inspiration for Lumina Grand , the 512-unit executive condo (EC) by City Developments Ltd (CDL) situated on Bukit Batok West Avenue 5.

Its architecture, by P&T Consultants, takes cues from the verticality and horizontal layering of a quarry, expressed through terraced forms and a series of frames that flow contiguously from the landscape deck to the clubhouses and up onto the residential blocks.

Meanwhile, the project’s landscape, helmed by Coen Design International, references the geological and ecological setting of the nearby Little Guilin, a nature park with a granite rock formation rising out of a lake.

Granite-inspired tiles in varying shades of grey are thus used across Lumina Grand.

The fully sold, completed project has picked up the Top Development and Top Executive Condominium accolades at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

These add to its earlier wins in 2024 for Top EC and Innovation Excellence in the uncompleted residential category.

Lumina Grand occupies a 99-year leasehold site at the junction of Bukit Batok West Avenue 5 and Bukit Batok Road.

Housed across 10 residential blocks, units range from 936 sq ft for a three-bedroom apartment to 1,711 sq ft for a five-bedder. The EC obtained its temporary occupation permit in April 2026.

Buyers were likely drawn to the project’s “attractive pricing, a reputable developer, efficient layout and quality finishes and appliances, within an estate that, although not formally classified as a mature estate, has rather established infrastructure and amenities”, says Sky Seah, senior lecturer at the Department of Real Estate, National University of Singapore, and an EPEA 2026 judge.

Lumina Grand made its market debut in January 2024, with 269 units, or 53% of the project, sold during the launch weekend at an average of $1,464 psf.

This August, CDL noted in its half-year financial results that all units at the development have been sold.

“Lumina Grand offers quality living at a price point that is affordable to its target market: mostly HDB upgraders and younger families,” Seah adds.

Flexible homes and wide range of facilities

The homes have been planned with flexibility in mind. Removable walls between living areas and bedrooms allow owners to alter their interior layouts for different uses and multigenerational households.

Most of the living rooms and bedrooms are oriented northeast or southwest, though two stacks of units near the entrance are designed to face southeast towards neighbouring greenery instead of the drop-off areas.

Larger four- and five-bedders have side-by-side living and dining areas. Smaller four-bedroom configurations were also created to cater to households that prefer a more compact unit but still want four rooms.

With about 40 facilities at the EC, residents have a wide range of options for wellness, leisure and social connection. They include a 50m lap pool, tennis court, gym, crafting pavilion, urban farming area, dance room, music room, reading lounges, lawns and gardens, as well as spaces for children and pets.

Its clubhouses can accommodate a variety of functions, such as gourmet kitchens, entertainment rooms, co-working lounges and studios — going beyond the typical condo function rooms.

Designed for easier upkeep

Lumina Grand’s design takes into account the upkeep of the property, with details meant to reduce maintenance needs and make future repair and replacement work easier.

For instance, horizontal projecting elements on the building façades have drip edges and grooves to reduce water streaking and the cleaning required.

The residential tower and clubhouse façades are made to be accessible for cleaning, maintenance and glass replacement.

Air-conditioning ledges are designed to make sure maintenance crews have sufficient working space and safety barriers.

Other measures focus on preventing water ingress and ponding — these include raised internal floor levels at entrances, sloped corridors and roofs, and upward-sloping floors at lift thresholds.

Green and smart living

Lumina Grand was conferred the BCA Green Mark Platinum Super Low Energy certification, supported by passive cooling design, energy-efficient appliances, renewable energy and smart home systems.

Its blocks are oriented to minimise direct west-facing exposure and encourage natural ventilation, while façade fins provide sun-shading.

Other sustainability measures include energy-efficient air-conditioning, lighting and lifts; water-efficient fittings; electric-vehicle charging stations; and renewable energy that partially offsets electricity consumption in common areas.

Smart-home features are provided within the apartments, including digital locks, remote air-conditioning and lighting controls, smart camera surveillance and monitoring of household energy consumption.

Residents can also use digital systems to pre-register visitors, book facilities and collect parcels.

The emphasis on smart living complements Lumina Grand’s location next to Tengah, Singapore’s first smart and sustainable HDB town, while residents at the EC may tap the array of amenities in the established Bukit Batok neighbourhood.

The development’s proximity to the Jurong Innovation District and Jurong Lake District also gives residents access to the two growing business hubs, with more jobs and infrastructure upgrades planned for western Singapore.

Connectivity is set to improve with the upcoming Tengah Park and Tengah Plantation MRT stations on the Jurong Region Line, in addition to the existing Bukit Gombak MRT Station on the North-South Line.

With its range of homes, facilities, flexible layouts and sustainability features, Lumina Grand caters to households at various stages of life, while benefitting from its Bukit Batok setting and the ongoing growth of the wider western region.

title: Copen Grand EC raises the bar for sustainable, smart living in Tengah
article:
As the first executive condo (EC) in Tengah, Copen Grand had an opportunity to set the standard for private residential living in the smart and sustainable new town.

The 639-unit development by City Developments Ltd (CDL) and Sunway MCL became the first EC to achieve the BCA Green Mark Platinum Super Low Energy certification, with sustainability incorporated into its design, construction and long-term maintenance.

Adding to its achievements in design and environmental performance, Copen Grand has clinched the Top Development award at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

The development comprises 12 residential blocks with two-bedroom-plus-study to five-bedroom units, complemented by extensive recreational facilities and smart-home features.

Located near Jurong Innovation District and Jurong Lake District, it is also within walking distance of three stations on the upcoming Jurong Region Line.

Launched in October 2022, the EC sold out within a month, ahead of its completion in April 2025.

Maintainability, sustainability built into its design

Designed for safe and more efficient maintenance from the outset, Copen Grand is also the first completed residential development to achieve the BCA Green Mark Maintainability Badge.

The development incorporates a multitude of Design for Maintainability features to ensure adequate and safe access for maintenance of areas such as roofs, façades, mechanical and electrical services rooms and tanks.

Residential blocks can be maintained using gondolas, while staircases provide access to the roofs and façades, supporting the development’s long-term maintenance needs.

Copen Grand also participated in the pilot bonus gross floor area (GFA) incentive scheme in 2021, securing an additional 2% bonus GFA through enhanced sustainability compliance and commitments, as well as technology- and productivity-driven measures across design, construction and management.

Solar panels installed on the residential tower roofs are estimated to generate 122,800 kWh of electricity annually, offsetting up to 30% of energy consumption in the common areas.

Other sustainability features include 20 electric-vehicle charging stations, demand-control strategies for lighting and air-conditioning at communal facilities, and a pneumatic waste conveyance system that channels refuse and recyclables from residential floor lobbies to a central collection point in the basement.

Architecturally, the master plan addresses the site’s irregular geometry by clustering the multi-storey car park with the main clubhouse facilities.

Rooftop landscaping on the car park creates a seamless, multi-level recreational zone that optimises the use of space and enhances site greenery beyond statutory requirements.

“The project’s design was able to tackle the site’s challenging context: an odd-shaped plot — literally a triangle — which was also flanked by an elevated MRT track on one side,” says Mark Ong, group director at P&T Consultants and an EPEA 2026 judge in the Design & Architecture specialisation.

A home for every generation

Taking its cue from Tengah’s “Forest Town” concept, Copen Grand’s landscaping brings residents closer to nature, with greenery woven through spaces for recreation, relaxation and community interaction.

From the ground-level drop-off, a series of staircases leads residents to a landscape deck elevated 4m above, where a “floating” clubhouse overlooks a water courtyard and cascading water wall.

At the fifth storey, a lush sky garden offers three zones catering to various ages and interests. The Play Zone has two playgrounds for children aged two to 12, while the Gardening Zone features edible plants and educational signage on plant species and their uses. The Fitness Zone houses an outdoor fitness corner, tennis court, putting green and a Sports Pavilion for rest.

On the main pool deck, a 50m lap pool is framed by tree canopies and pool loungers. Nearby, the hydrotherapy pool offers a more secluded setting, with aqua massage jets and jacuzzi alcoves.

These are among more than 45 recreational facilities spread across eight clubs.

Residents also have access to co-working spaces, study pods, a children’s clubhouse, yoga and dance studios, a games room, an entertainment room with karaoke facilities, a pet corner and scented gardens.

Designed for comfort and flexibility

Inside the homes, colour schemes inspired by Tengah’s natural surroundings are combined with practical finishes and features intended for everyday living.

All residential towers are positioned in a true north-south orientation to minimise direct east-west solar heat gain, with openings facing north and south for better cross-ventilation.

Within the residential units, 60% of applicable spaces are designed with unobstructed airflow between internal spaces and the outside.

Other climate-responsive considerations at Copen Grand include naturally ventilated corridors and lobbies, as well as glass specifications to minimise solar heat gain. The use of internal wall paints with low levels of volatile organic compounds also reduces indoor air pollution.

The homes come with fittings from Rigel and Grohe, while porcelain tiles resembling natural stone are used in living and dining areas and bathrooms for durability and ease of maintenance, coupled with a touch of refined elegance.

Rounded corners in cabinetry enhance safety, particularly for families with young children, while storage niches are incorporated at entrances, kitchen islands and within wardrobes.

Hackable walls give homeowners flexibility as their needs and lifestyles change. Young couples can create a larger living area for entertaining, a hobby room or a work-from-home space, while growing families can reconfigure their layout to accommodate a nursery, or for multigenerational living.

Smart technology for holistic living

Technology brings added convenience to daily living at the EC.

Each apartment has a Smart Hub gateway that allows homeowners to remotely control appliances such as air-conditioning and lighting through a mobile app.

A Smart Power Monitoring system also enables residents to track household energy consumption.

Together with its green design, recreational facilities and provisions for long-term maintenance, these features bring Tengah’s vision of smart and sustainable living into Copen Grand’s residential environment.

title: AMO Residence sets new benchmark for suburban living in Ang Mo Kio
article:
It has been one year since AMO Residence , a 372-unit private residential development in the mature Ang Mo Kio estate, was completed. The development received its temporary occupation permit in October 2025, about three years after its launch made a splash in the property market.

The development by UOL Group , together with joint-venture partners Singapore Land Group Ltd (SingLand) and Kheng Leong Co, shifted 98% of its units on the first day of launch in July 2022.

The developers sold the last unit at AMO Residence — a 678 sq ft two-bedder on the 16th floor that fetched 1.6million(2,359 psf) — in April 2025. On average, units at the fully sold project transacted at $2,116 psf, caveats show.

AMO Residence’s performance helped set the tone for subsequent launches in the Outside Central Region, particularly in the nearby Lentor Hills area, recalls Desmond Sim, former group CEO of Realion (OrangeTee and ETC) Group and a judge for the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

“In a way, it set a precedent for the Lentor Hills estate, because Lentor Modern was launched after that,” he says. The integrated development with 605 residences was the first project to launch in the emerging neighbourhood in September 2022. It is now fully taken up, with prices averaging at $2,107 psf.

At the EPEA 2026, AMO Residence walked away with two wins — Innovation Excellence and Top Development — for completed residential projects.

Sought-after plot

AMO Residence is located at Ang Mo Kio Rise, a cul-de-sac off Ang Mo Kio Avenue 1 that was built as the project’s main access point. Visitors walking or driving up Ang Mo Kio Rise to the condo’s main entrance will see the development’s twin 25-storey residential blocks rising elegantly.

The glass-clad, slightly staggered towers are a sleek addition to the surrounding buildings, which largely comprise landed housing off Ang Mo Kio Avenue 2 and the Kebun Baru HDB blocks.

The condo occupies a 136,480 sq ft, 99-year leasehold site that the developers purchased through a Government Land Sale tender in June 2021. At the time, Ang Mo Kio had not seen a new private residential launch in eight years, making the plot an enticing prospect to tap pent-up demand. Ang Mo Kio’s rich amenities, coupled with the site’s proximity to an MRT station, further enhanced its appeal.

The site is a five-minute walk from the Mayflower MRT Station on the Thomson-East Coast Line. Additionally, it is close to Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park and Lower Peirce Reservoir Park, as well as reputable schools such as Ai Tong School on Bright Hill Drive and CHIJ St Nicholas Girls’ School, which are within 1km of the project.

As a result, competition for the site was stiff. Fifteen bids were received for the parcel, with the UOL-led joint venture coming out on top with its offer of 381.83million(1,118 psf per plot ratio).

Built for an immersive lifestyle

AMO Residence’s plot has a slight gradient, which the developers used to their advantage. “The site is upward-sloping, and the developers used the terrain to create multi-level activities and landscaping,” highlights EPEA judge Sim.

Guided by the site’s inherent qualities and the nature offerings close by, emphasis was placed on keeping the building footprint small in exchange for more landscaping and facilities, with the latter making up over 60% of the plot.

Water bodies account for a significant portion of the landscaping, including a 50m lap pool, a recreational pool, an aquatherapy pool and a kids’ pool. With the exception of the lap pool, they feature organic shapes surrounded by dense and diverse greenery to evoke the scenic settings of reservoirs.

Other facilities provided are a thoughtful mix, including three function rooms, a tennis court, outdoor dining spaces, a pet area, a gym and social space, and multiple lawns and decks.

Altogether, they offer a generous range of amenities built for residents to enjoy a balanced and immersive lifestyle.

AMO Residence was designed by Singapore architectural and engineering practice P&T Consultants. STX Landscape Architects did the landscape design, while multidisciplinary design studio Index Design worked on the interiors.

Choice units

Homes at AMO Residence come in a wide variety of layouts, ranging from two- to five-bedders between 614 and 1,475 sq ft. The largest units are the condo’s three simplex penthouses, sized between 2,293 and 2,497 sq ft.

Helpful features were integrated into the homes, such as a niche in two-bedroom premium units that can be used as a small work area or additional storage space. Three-bedders and above come with an enclosed kitchen, while four– and five-bedroom units come with private lifts.

Over half the units have unblocked views, with homes facing northwards having views spanning landed enclaves and Lower Peirce Reservoir Park. Southward-facing units have views towards Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park.

With its thoughtful design centred around well-appointed homes, greenery and quality lifestyle amenities, AMO Residence serves as a fine addition to the established Ang Mo Kio neighbourhood.

title: Completed Tembusu Grand wins praise for  liveable homes, green credentials
article:
Residents at Tembusu Grand , a 638-unit residential development off Tanjong Katong Road, started collecting keys for their newly completed units at the end of last year. The condo obtained its temporary occupation permit in December, followed by its certificate of completion earlier this year.

The project was delivered around three years after it was launched. The 99-year leasehold development, a joint venture between City Developments Ltd (CDL) and Sunway MCL (then known as MCL Land), commenced sales in April 2023.

The project’s completion has been followed by triple honours at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

Judges crowned the development with the Sustainability Excellence and Top Development titles. Tembusu Grand also clinched the People’s Choice award — determined by online votes from the general public — for completed residential projects.

The wins add to the project’s impressive track record at the EPEA. Tembusu Grand previously bagged five awards in the uncompleted category: Design Excellence, Innovation Excellence, Marketing Excellence, Showflat Excellence and the People’s Choice award.

Smart layout

Tembusu Grand’s completion brings to life a unique design inspired by the tembusu tree from which it gets its name and address. Located along Jalan Tembusu, the development features four residential towers rising 20 to 21 storeys.

From the exterior, observers will see sculptural crowns on the two blocks closest to the main entrance — a nod to the tembusu tree’s distinctive silhouette and wide-spreading canopy.

Upon entering the development, residents and visitors are greeted by a large drop-off area with an art installation and other decorative elements.

Farther in, an extensive network of water bodies lies at the heart of the site, anchored by the 50m lap pool. The residential blocks run parallel on either side, while a clubhouse sits at each end of the pools.

More facilities, such as the tennis court and co-working space, are located on Level 5, above the condo’s multi-storey carpark.

“Many of the front-facing components, such as the arrival area and other common spaces, are effectively used to conceal the project’s back-of-house components,” Mark Ong, group director at architecture and engineering firm P&T Consultants, highlights.

The placement of the buildings creates a courtyard formation that accommodates gardens and other landscaping, Ng Sze Oun, director at landscape studio Compound Creative, adds.

Both Ong and Ng sat on the judging panel for this year’s EPEA.

Modern, elegant homes

Tembusu Grand was designed by ADDP Architects. The acclaimed Singapore practice has collaborated with CDL on several projects, such as the 429-unit Tree House condo on Chestnut Avenue and Lucerne Grande, CDL’s 570-unit project on Lakeside Drive that launched in October.

ADDP Architects also designed CDL’s other joint-venture projects with Sunway MCL: the 407-unit Piccadilly Grand in Farrer Park; and the 639-unit Copen Grand , the first executive condo in Tengah Town. The fully sold developments were both completed last year.

For Tembusu Grand, ADDP Architects collaborated with interior designer JOW Architects and landscape architect Tinderbox.

Tembusu Grand’s residences range from one-bedroom-plus-study apartments of 527 sq ft to five-bedders of 1,711 sq ft. The largest units are the two five-bedroom penthouses of 2,691 sq ft.

All apartments come with premium appliances from Miele, Liebherr and Smeg in the kitchens, along with Hansgrohe and Geberit fittings in the bathrooms. Each unit also features a smart home system that includes a video doorbell as well as air conditioning and lighting controls.

Tembusu Grand is now 99% sold, based on caveats lodged as at Oct 28. Units at the condo fetched an average price of around $2,440 psf.

Elevated amenities

Tembusu Grand residents have access to an impressive array of facilities. In addition to customary provisions such as function rooms and barbecue areas, the developers curated a well-rounded mix of lifestyle amenities to cater to residents’ different needs.

These include four pools (the 50m lap pool, a smaller Relaxing Pool, a kids’ pool and a spa pool), a co-working lounge, a yoga studio, and a kids’ playroom and playhouse.

The Grand Club, one of the development’s two clubhouses, features an entertainment room, a function room and karaoke and gaming pods.

The other clubhouse, called Tembusu Club, features a private dining area and observation deck. It is attached to the gym, which is cantilevered from the fifth storey of the multi-storey carpark and overlooks the condo grounds.

The facilities are elevated by Tembusu Grand’s lush landscaping. Waterscapes are a running theme throughout the development, with the pool areas complemented by several ornamental water features.

These include water cascades near the arrival zone and below the gym, a lily pond that surrounds a sunken seating area by the lap pool, and a water courtyard next to the gym.

Open lawns, thematic gardens and a vast array of plants and trees round out the condo’s verdant landscapes. Green turf also covers the roofs of the clubhouses and other low-rise buildings, amplifying the multi-layered greenery.

Green features

Tembusu Grand won the Sustainability Excellence award at the EPEA this year in recognition of its green features.

Both passive and active design strategies were used to incorporate eco -friendly features. These include the residential blocks’ north-south orientation to promote ventilation and reduce heat transfer, as well as extensive green and blue spaces.

Tembusu Grand’s construction also utilised sustainable building materials and systems.

Among the provisions are energy- and water-efficient fittings and appliances, electric-vehicle charging stations and bicycle lots. There is also a pneumatic waste collection and disposal system, as well as motion sensors in the common areas to reduce electricity wastage.

The project has a Platinum Super Low Energy certification, among the highest accolades under the Building and Construction Authority’s Green Mark rating system.

Overall, EPEA judges were impressed by Tembusu Grand’s attentive design that responds to the needs of homebuyers. “It’s an estate that I can totally imagine residents would be happy to live in,” says P&T Consultants’ Ong.

title: Jervois Mansion's nature-inspired, community-driven design wins three awards at EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards 2026
article:
A resident at Jervois Mansion recently approached Edmund Eng, associate director of developer Kimen Group , with an unusual complaint. The rooftop laundry area was so popular that she could never find space to hang her bedsheets.

Eng checked with the condo manager and discovered that the morning slots were usually taken, leaving latecomers to wait until lunchtime or the afternoon. He has since suggested putting up a notice reminding residents to collect their laundry once it is dry, so others can have their turn.

It was quite a turnaround from just 10 months earlier, when the 130-unit freehold development was newly completed at the end of 2025. Back then, Eng had to encourage residents to use the rooftop laundry facilities, which include two commercial-grade washing machines and drying racks, instead of hanging laundry on their balconies.

The rooftop laundry area may seem like an unconventional amenity for a luxury condo. Yet it reflects the philosophy behind Jervois Mansion. Its architecture, landscaping, and communal spaces are designed to bring residents together while preserving the charm and character of the District 10 enclave.

The development by Kimen Group won three honours at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards 2026: Design Excellence, Landscape Excellence, and Top Development in the completed projects category.

The latest accolades follow its wins for Landscape Excellence and Top Development in the uncompleted projects category at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards 2022.

Reviving the spirit of community

The inspiration for the rooftop laundry area came from two experiences that left a lasting impression on Arthur Aw, executive director of Kimen Group.

The first was during a business trip to India many years ago, when Aw observed how rooftop laundry areas had become informal gathering places. “You see people hanging up their clothes to dry, and then stopping to chat or gossip with their neighbours,” he recalls.

The second experience was closer to home, at the original Jervois Mansions, a 32-unit condo completed in 1985. Expatriate tenants asked Aw, whose family owned the development, whether there was an area for their domestic helpers to socialise. He identified a corner for them, and it soon became a popular gathering place.

The redevelopment was also deeply personal for Aw. His father, Aw Kim Chen, founded the property business Aw & Sons in 1971, along with its affiliate Kimen Group. In 1980, Aw senior acquired three bungalows along Jervois Road and redeveloped the site into Jervois Mansions.

Aw was 18 when he helped out at the Jervois Mansions construction site before enlisting for National Service. He remembers cycling through the surrounding Good Class Bungalow (GCB) neighbourhood to reach the site.

“I thought it was such a nice, unique environment, with the GCBs and the colonial-era black-and-white bungalows,” he recalls.

Those early impressions would eventually shape his vision for the new Jervois Mansion.

A trained architect, Aw held senior planning and development roles at JTC, Ascendas and Ascendas-Singbridge, including overseeing the design and planning of one-north, before joining the family business at Kimen Group in 2018.

By then, Aw had decided it was time to redevelop Jervois Mansions. The condo was more than 30 years old, increasingly dated and “under-optimised” in terms of market value, he says.

Redeveloping the site allowed Kimen Group to maximise its potential and create value beyond gross floor area (GFA). More importantly, it would “unlock the war chest needed to build a real estate brand”, says Aw.

From experimental garden to rooftop urban farm

Before the original Jervois Mansions was demolished at the end of 2021, Aw had already begun using parts of the site as a testing ground for ideas that would eventually be incorporated into the redevelopment.

Together with Mason Tan, landscape architect and managing director of Mace Studio, and biodiversity planner Janet Wong, Aw experimented with different planting techniques and materials.

These included growing moss in 12mm gaps between paving stones — a feature subsequently incorporated into the driveway of Jervois Mansion — testing edible plants under different soil conditions and experimenting with soilless turf.

The experiments piqued the curiosity of residents, particularly children. “The moment the plants began to grow, the expatriate children would gather around,” recalls Tan.

What began as a small experimental garden has since evolved into the rooftop urban farm and landscape design at Jervois Mansion.

Today, residents can find edible plants ranging from lime and kedondong (golden apple) to kuchai (Chinese chives), long beans and lady’s finger (okra). About 60% of the rooftop plants are either edible or have medicinal qualities, according to Wong of Mace Studio. “They have been used traditionally, but as urban dwellers, we have forgotten about them,” she says.

Tan and Wong intend to organise regular guided tours around the condo, introducing residents to plants that can be harvested for food, traditional medicinal uses or floral arrangements at home.

Creating intimacy through courtyards

The architectural design was led by Christopher Lee, co-founder and principal of London-based Serie Architects.

“It’s a very unusual collaboration between a client and architect,” says Lee of his working relationship with Aw. “Sometimes, it’s almost as if we were in the same office. We bounce ideas off each other and critique them. It’s a very comfortable relationship.”

One of their earliest debates centred on the orientation of the five-storey residential blocks.

“The default response for both architects and developers is generally that the bigger the open space, the more desirable the development,” says Lee.

However, studies of the Jervois Mansion site showed that maximising a single open space would mean arranging the blocks in a line or an L-shape. Despite the generous open area, the result would feel “quite oppressive”, with a monotonous wall of apartments overlooking a featureless space, Lee explains.

Instead, the buildings were organised around three courtyards, creating a sequence of outdoor spaces that gradually unfolds as residents move through the development.

“That sense of moving from room to room in an outdoor space is quite a distinctive departure from the kind of five-storey development you typically see in Singapore,” says Lee.

The courtyards have what Lee describes as “very European proportions”, with their height and width carefully calibrated to create a more intimate setting.

The same attention was given to the interiors. Aw brought in interior designer Gwen Tan, founder and principal of Studio iF and co-founder and partner of Formwerkz Design Collective, before the building plans had been finalised.

Much of the design process took place in 1Q2020 during the Covid-19 lockdown, which prompted the team to consider how residents might use their homes and shared spaces in the future.

The design team also drew inspiration from Aw's memories of the Jervois neighbourhood and its black-and-white bungalows. That common vision influenced everything from the architecture and interior layouts to the lobbies, landscaping and drop-off area.

Even the orientation of individual apartments and the placement of their windows were carefully measured to balance views and privacy, adds Lee.

For Aw, the design’s success lies partly in details residents may not consciously notice. “They’ll just think it’s nice,” he says. “They don’t realise it’s the little things, where the interior design blends with the architecture, that create that sense of comfort.”

Designing for long-term maintenance

While the architecture and landscaping are among Jervois Mansion's most visible features, considerable effort also went into ensuring that they would remain practical to maintain.

One of the development’s distinctive features is its façade, where cascading tropical creepers spill from planter boxes built into individual apartments.

Keeping that greenery healthy and maintaining it safely fell to Tan Wee Teck, founder and managing director of Project Management International (PMI), who joined the project as quality director.

Before committing to the design, he decided to test it. “If it’s nice to look at, but hard to maintain, then it defeats the purpose,” he says.

Tan built a mock-up of the planter box on the balcony of a workers' dormitory project he was overseeing at the time, when Jervois Mansion was still in its concept phase.

He arranged for a worker using a gondola to reach the planter box suspended on the fifth floor — equivalent to the top level of Jervois Mansion — to assess how easily it could be maintained.

The exercise led to the installation of gondola anchor slots at 3m intervals across all six residential blocks, allowing access to approximately 95% of the façades.

Besides tending the planters every four months, the gondola can also be used for annual glass-panel washing and façade repainting every five to six years, adds Tan.

The interconnected rooftops of the six residential blocks are organised into different zones for recreational and communal activities. Beneath the rooftop facilities is a double-slab system designed to channel rainwater towards downpipes and provide additional waterproofing protection.

Another less visible feature is the environmental deck, where drainage cells beneath the planting areas help detain rainwater, supplementing the conventional detention tank in the basement.

The same emphasis on quality influenced the selection of the main contractor. Although Singapore Engineering & Construction did not submit the lowest bid, it was ultimately appointed to undertake the project.

“We didn't want short-term gain in the form of higher profit margin, but face more maintenance issues further down the road,” says PMI's Tan.

Jervois Mansion subsequently achieved the Building and Construction Authority's Green Mark GoldPlus Super Low Energy certification for new residential buildings.

A long-term commitment

Kimen Group also engaged Roxy-Pacific Holdings as development manager, drawing on its experience in boutique residential projects and compact apartments.

The development's unit mix was designed to appeal to different buyer segments. More compact one- and two-bedroom apartments starting from 495 sq ft were intended to offer relatively accessible price points for younger buyers and those with family ties to the prime District 10 neighbourhood.

At the other end of the spectrum , Aw opted for larger three- and four-bedroom apartments of up to 2,271 sq ft.

Kimen Group has retained an entire block comprising 25 of these larger units for investment, rather than selling every apartment in the development.

All 25 units retained by Kimen Group have been leased. In September, a four-bedroom apartment measuring approximately 2,000 to 2,100 sq ft fetched $17,600 a month, setting a new rental benchmark for Jervois Mansion, based on URA data.

For Eng, the rooftop laundry area is one of the clearest examples of Jervois Mansion’s design philosophy in everyday life. A small table and chairs let residents sit and chat while they wait for their laundry, and at the adjacent urban farm, a pavilion has a long table that seats eight.

“In the evenings, I see a lot of conversations taking place there, and many friendships forged among neighbours,” he says. “Every time I have VIP visitors, the first thing they comment on is the laundry area. They say it’s like a kampong.”

title: Why real estate rivals applaud each other's success
article:
The 10th anniversary celebration of the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards brings together stakeholders from across the industry to honour excellence in real estate development.

I am honoured to have served on the judging panel for the past four years. In that time, a few notable changes have occurred: the range of property types has widened, submissions now come from beyond our shores, and, most significantly, public-sector participation has increased.

With projects such as Punggol Digital District and Bidadari Park winning awards, their recognition brings into public view years, even decades, of planning and coordination that would otherwise go unnoticed.

That business rivals would gather to applaud one another’s success may surprise those who take a zero-sum view of competition: that profit-maximising firms should treat a competitor’s success as their own loss.

Yet my years of interaction with veterans in the real estate field have consistently shown me that the best among us aspire to contribute to the collective good.

A rival’s good work lifts the whole industry. The standard of one raises the standard of all.

The celebration epitomises the nature of real estate development, an entrepreneurial activity that is inherently collaborative. No project is built by one hand.

Ask any practitioner about seeing a difficult project come to fruition . They will speak with a parent’s pride and quickly acknowledge the many hands behind it.

Each project shapes the social and economic environment that shapes it. A collaborative, cooperative culture mirrors how development is built and underpins the real estate practice.

Building a city together

Singapore’s economic success cannot be separated from its urban development, within which the real estate sector plays an integral role.

Notwithstanding its size, the city-state has always marched to the beat of its own drum. Since independence, the country has pursued place-based policies with conviction even as economists continue to debate the relative merits of place-based and people-based policies.

Place-based policies target investment and public resources towards specific locations, whereas people-based policies support individuals regardless of where they reside.

In Singapore, place-based policies are largely implemented through an institutional framework of urban planning, development control and land administration.

While the government ensures that all developments contribute to the wider national economic, social and community goals through the provision of infrastructure and urban services, the private sector has always been indispensable in the supply of entrepreneurial inputs in areas of market knowledge, financial resources and design expertise.

As was true in the past, so it is now: Singapore’s development continues to be an active exercise in public-private partnership.

At this 10th anniversary, it is fitting to remember that real estate is more than an asset class. It is a product that accomplishes far more, embedding social value, generating wealth, creating positive externalities and building communities. Each development is understood to have the potential to contribute to something larger than the project itself.

From the speeches by the chief executives of the award-winning developments on the night of the award ceremony, it is clear that leaders in the real estate profession recognise not only their obligations to investors and buyers, but also their social responsibilities to the public and future generations.

Why judges return

Recognition that is given to everyone honours no one, so the integrity of an award must be upheld.

A judging panel that quietly serves the vested interests of its own members erodes trust and goodwill. Judging is effortful and rightly uncompensated. The cost in time is real, yet in some cases, judges return year after year.

What gives? While real estate is a business, at its best, it is also a form of stewardship. Its decisions are multifaceted, enduring and often irreversible, so a good steward sees a project through the eyes of everyone it touches.

An investor sees risk and return, a planner sees environmental and community impact, a resident sees liveability, and a neighbour sees change on their street, for better or for worse.

Judging offers a rare chance to hone that skill, stepping into each stakeholder’s perspective, then weighing those perspectives towards the best possible outcome.

Perhaps it was the continual perspective-taking within our panel of judges that led to serendipity; we became friends. In the third spaces where we gather, camaraderie is born. A diorama within a diorama, real estate people in a real estate space, talking real estate.

Competition and cooperation are not opposites. An award tradition that celebrates excellence embodies both and helps raise the reputation and standards of the industry.

Year after year, the award ceremony reminds us of this purposeful industry to which we belong, a multifaceted industry that brings together the talents of many fields, capable of transforming the ambitions of a city and its residents into reality.

Congratulations to Bernard Tong and his EdgeProp Singapore team . May the next 10 years build on the strong foundation you have created and take the industry higher still.

title: Ten years and 550 submissions later, we have learnt to ask better questions
article:
Distinguished guests, Dato’ Sris, Datos, ladies and gentlemen. Good evening and welcome to the 10th EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards .

Ten years. For those of you who have been with us since the very first year, it also means you have had to sit through my speech 10 times.

And judging by tonight’s turnout, I clearly have not scared enough of you away. We have a record 408 guests tonight — our largest gathering ever. Thank you all for being here.

How the awards have evolved

When we first started, these awards were largely about homes. Since then, they have grown to cover integrated developments, hotels, co-living and, most recently, commercial and industrial developments.

Last year, we welcomed JTC as the first government agency to take part in the awards. And this year, we are very pleased to welcome Singapore’s Housing and Development Board (HDB).

This is important for a real estate award, because great placemaking is not confined to private developments. It can also be a public park, or a shared space, that brings a community together.

And for the first time this year, we are giving out awards beyond Singapore, opening them up to overseas markets such as Malaysia and Australia, where many Singaporeans are buying homes.

What we have learnt: asking better questions

Now, if there’s one thing we have learnt from organising these awards over the years, after reviewing over 550 submissions, it’s that we have learnt to ask better questions.

I still remember, when we first started doing site visits, one of our favourite questions was: “What’s the monthly maintenance fee?”

But over time, as we visited more developments and listened to the architects, designers and developers explain their projects, we began to appreciate just how much thought goes into a building.

Almost every design decision involves a trade-off.

For example, how do you balance privacy with openness? How do you add sustainable features while keeping costs manageable? How do you maximise efficiency without compromising on liveability?

There is rarely a perfect answer, and I don’t envy the jobs of those making these tough decisions.

This year, during one of our site visits, we had a rather unusual opportunity. A resident at Jervois Mansion , a site we visited, kindly invited us into his home, where we met his family — including his son and their dog.

It was a lovely home. They were living comfortably, enjoying the space and the beautiful view from their balcony.

I am not entirely sure the dog appreciated the view. But then again, he does not have to pay the maintenance fees.

Jokes aside, that visit was a nice reminder of why we do this.

We have spent a lot of time examining designs, layouts, landscaping, materials and facilities. But ultimately, these are places where people live, where children grow up, and where families make memories.

And perhaps that’s the most important thing we have learnt over the past decade: A great development is not just about how it looks or how efficient it is, but how well it works for the people living in it.

What has not changed: integrity

While a lot has changed over 10 years, one thing has not — our commitment to the integrity of these awards.

Our judges have spent countless hours reviewing submissions, both quantitative and qualitative, visiting sites and debating over each development.  Every result is independently reviewed by our knowledge partners, KPMG and CPG.

Because ultimately, an award is only as meaningful as what goes behind it.

Closing: something old, new, borrowed and blue

Ten years together with many of you in this room — at this point, it’s practically like a marriage. So I thought I would end my speech by borrowing a traditional wedding saying: something old, something new, something borrowed and something blue.

Something old — the friendships and partnerships we have built over the past decade. Partners like Mitsubishi Electric and KPMG, who have been with us since our very first awards in 2017, and V-Zug, Geberit and CPG, and Mr Khew Sin Khoon, who have stood with us for years since. Thank you for believing in these awards from the start.

Something new — the new categories, new markets and new frontiers we will keep exploring over the next 10 years. And the new friends joining us on that journey: Avatr, our official automotive partner; our supporting partners, the Kurater and The Sourcing King; and our agency partners — PropNex, ERA, Huttons, OrangeTee and SRI. Thank you for believing in us and welcome to the family.

Something borrowed — here, I must thank the countless hours and wisdom we have borrowed from our judges, many of whom will step down from the judging panel next year.  Beyond the work, we have also learnt a lot about one another over lunches, coffee, beer and ducks.

And finally, something blue — that’s my team, in EdgeProp blue.  My job tonight is easy, I just had to use ChatGPT to write my speech, but they are the ones who have spent months chasing submissions, coordinating site visits, keeping our judges fed and on schedule, and making sure tonight runs smoothly.  Please give them a round of applause.

To everyone who has been part of this journey, thank you for your trust and continued support.

And to all our finalists and winners tonight — congratulations. Your work continues to inspire us, and I can’t wait to see what the next 10 years will bring.

Thank you, and enjoy the evening!

Bernard Tong, CEO of EdgeProp Singapore

title: Beyond Blue Chips: 3 Hidden Gems Beating the STI’s Red October
article:
Singapore’s blue chips had a rough October.
The
SPDR STI ETF
(SGX: ES3), which mirrors the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), delivered a total return of negative 5.5% for the month.
When the broader market pulls back like this, it is easy to assume everything on the exchange is sliding down the same slope.
Yet not every stock followed the benchmark lower.
Old Chang Kee
(SGX: 5ML), or OCK, delivered a total return of 1.7%.
Civmec
(SGX: P9D) returned 1.4%, while
Tai Sin Electric
(SGX: 500) returned 1.0%.
These are total returns, so they capture dividends as well as share price moves.
Granted, gains of one or two percent might look modest on paper.
But standing in stark contrast to a sea of red across the STI, they naturally catch an investor’s eye.
So what did these three
small caps
have going for them?
One month proves little on its own.
Look a little closer, however, and each company offers investors something concrete to hold on to when the broader market turns chilly.
What can a curry puff maker offer in a falling market?
OCK is practically a household name across Singapore, best known for its signature deep-fried curry puffs.
Beyond its familiar retail snack kiosks at high-traffic MRT stations and shopping malls, the group also generates revenue through food delivery, catering services and business-to-business supply channels.
For its fiscal year ended 31 March 2026 (FY2026), OCK grew revenue by 1.5% year on year (YoY) to S$103.5 million.
Profit went the other way.
Net profit attributable to shareholders fell 15.8% YoY to S$9.6 million as wage adjustments, higher depreciation and lower interest income took their toll.
So where’s the comfort for investors?
It’s the cash.
As at 31 March 2026, OCK held S$61.6 million in cash and deposits against just S$1.4 million of debt.
In other words, it had net cash of around S$60 million.
The group also generated S$21.0 million of free cash flow in FY2026, down from S$23.2 million a year earlier.
OCK declared an interim dividend of S$0.01 and proposed a final dividend of S$0.01.
On top of these ordinary dividends, the board proposed a special dividend of S$0.01.
Looking ahead, management expects inflationary pressure and local manpower shortages to remain persistent headwinds.
OCK plans to counter these operational hurdles by tightening cost controls and expanding its non-retail sales channels.
Can Civmec’s order book carry the momentum?
Civmec, headquartered in Henderson, Western Australia, provides engineering, construction and naval shipbuilding services to the energy, resources, infrastructure, and marine and defence sectors.
For the first quarter of its fiscal year ending 30 June 2027 (1QFY2027), Civmec grew revenue by 70.2% YoY to a record A$324.0 million, up from A$190.4 million a year earlier.
Net profit after tax surged 75.2% YoY to A$18.4 million.
The group’s construction division spearheaded this rapid expansion as major project work for resource giants like BHP Group Limited and Iluka Resources Limited ramped up significantly.
The order book gives investors a view of the work ahead.
It stood at around A$1.4 billion at the end of the quarter, up from A$1.15 billion a year prior.
Building on that momentum, the group announced on 5 October 2026 that it had secured additional contract awards and extensions worth over A$220 million.
Shareholders also received Civmec’s final dividend of A$0.035 per share for FY2026 on 23 October 2026, bringing total dividends declared for that financial year to A$0.060.
Investors should keep two gaps in view.
The quarterly update didn’t include a cash flow statement or balance sheet, so the quarter’s free cash flow remains unknown.
Management also gave no financial guidance for FY2027.
Why might investors look past Tai Sin’s profit slump?
Tai Sin
makes and distributes electrical cables and wires across Southeast Asia.
It also runs electrical-product distribution, testing and inspection and renewable energy businesses.
For its fiscal year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), Tai Sin grew revenue by 24.2% YoY to S$597.2 million.
Its renewable energy division, acquired back in November 2025, made an immediate impact by contributing S$59.8 million to that revenue total.
Profitability, however, took a severe hit.
Net profit attributable to equity holders plunged 56.8% YoY to S$11.2 million.
Here’s the thing: most of the damage came from a S$23.1 million provision for onerous contracts.
Tai Sin had signed long-term, fixed-price cable contracts when copper was cheaper.
Copper prices have since risen and those contracts now lose money.
The good news?
The provision is a non-cash charge, so cash flow held up.
Operating cash flow staged a dramatic recovery to S$16.7 million, reversing an outflow of S$5.2 million a year earlier.
Free cash flow similarly swung back into positive territory at S$9.0 million, compared with negative S$9.9 million in FY2025.
That matters, because free cash flow is what ultimately pays for
dividends
.
Tai Sin kept its final dividend unchanged at S$0.016 per share, leaving its total full-year dividend steady at S$0.0235 per share.
The risks are real, though. Bank borrowings rose to S$106.2 million from S$84.4 million as the group paid for its acquisition and pricier copper.
As at 30 June 2026, Tai Sin had S$44.6 million in cash.
Further increases in copper prices could also trigger more provisions.
Get Smart: Test the anchor, not the month
It feels good to own a stock that made money while the STI ETF lost 5.5%.
But one good month tells you very little about the next.
A better question is how much weight each anchor can bear.
OCK’s cash already sits on its balance sheet, while Civmec still has to deliver on its order book.
Tai Sin’s cash flow improved, but its borrowings and copper exposure grew too.
So before you buy a stock just because it held up in a bad month, ask yourself this: if the STI keeps sliding, which of these anchors would you still trust?

title: Ahead of DBS’s Earnings: 3 Key Metrics Investors Must Watch
article:
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) reports its third-quarter results for 2026 (3Q2026) on 5 November 2026.
Most investors will head straight for the profit figure.
You may want to look at the mix behind it instead.
Here’s the thing: lower interest rates are squeezing what Singapore’s largest lender earns from lending.
Fees are filling the gap.
The coming results will tell us whether that trade-off still works.
Where does DBS stand after the second quarter?
For context, 2Q2026 was a
milestone quarter
.
Total income rose 6% year on year (YoY) to S$6.1 billion.
It was the first time total income crossed the S$6 billion mark.
Profit before allowances grew 8% to a record S$3.7 billion.
Net profit attributable to shareholders rose 9% to S$3.1 billion.
That works out to a return on equity of 17.9%.
Dig a little deeper and you’ll find two very different trends.
Net interest income (NII) slipped 2% YoY to S$3.6 billion.
Non-interest income went the other way – it rose 21% to S$2.5 billion.
How much further can the net interest margin fall?
The net interest margin (NIM) is the gap between what DBS earns on its loans and what it pays for its funding.
In 2Q2026, DBS’s NIM narrowed by 18 basis points to 1.87%, down from 2.05% a year ago.
Lower interest rates were the culprit.
Hedging and balance sheet growth softened the blow.
So treat 1.87% as your baseline.
If NIM holds near that level on 5 November, the squeeze may be easing.
If it narrows again, DBS will need its other income streams to work even harder.
Can DBS lend its way past thinner margins?
Partly, yes.
Customer loans grew 8% YoY to S$469.4 billion in 2Q2026.
Lending to large corporates made up most of the increase.
When DBS earns less on each dollar it lends, it needs to lend more dollars.
That extra lending helped cushion the dip in NII.
Growth only counts if the loans stay good.
In 2Q2026, the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio stayed unchanged at 1.0%.
Watch whether DBS can keep growing its loan book at a similar pace without that ratio creeping up.
Can wealth management keep carrying the load?
This may be the metric that matters most.
Non-interest income rose 21% YoY to S$2.5 billion in 2Q2026.
Net fee and commission income grew 25% to S$1.5 billion.
Within fees, wealth management was the standout.
Its fees climbed 42% to S$919 million.
Treasury customer sales and other income also increased 30% to S$681 million.
Management expects wealth management to drive mid-teens growth in commercial book non-interest income for 2026.
Note that this guidance covers only the commercial book.
You can’t compare it directly with the group’s 21% figure.
That said, 42% growth sets a high bar.
For the third quarter, the question is whether wealth fees can keep growing fast enough to support management’s guidance.
Don’t count on 42% every quarter.
What has management promised for 2026?
When DBS released its 2Q results, management raised its full-year guidance.
DBS now expects 2026 total income to exceed 2025 levels.
It also expects mid-teens growth in commercial book non-interest income.
The 3Q numbers will show whether the bank
remains on track
to deliver both.
What did shareholders receive?
For 2Q2026, the board declared two separate
payouts
:
Interim dividend: S$0.66 per share
Capital return dividend: S$0.15 per share
The interim dividend is the ordinary payout.
The capital return dividend sits apart from it.
If you’re a dividend investor, the number to watch in 3Q is whether the board keeps the interim dividend at S$0.66.
What could go wrong?
The biggest risk is that lower interest rates keep pressing down on NIM.
If loan growth slows at the same time, DBS loses part of its cushion.
Wealth management carries its own risk.
Fee income depends on client activity, and 2Q’s 42% growth leaves little room for disappointment.
A slowdown here would make the full-year guidance harder to hit.
Get Smart: Watch the two engines side by side
When DBS reports on 5 November, resist the urge to jump straight to net profit.
Look at two numbers first.
Check the change in NII, and then check the change in non-interest income.
In 2Q2026, non-interest income grew 21% while NII fell 2%.
That gap helps explain how net profit still rose 9%.
If fee growth keeps outpacing the margin squeeze, DBS’s shift in its earnings mix is working.
If the gap narrows, the squeeze becomes the bigger story.
And as a dividend investor, that’s the story you’ll want to follow.

title: Asian tech stocks to rise on AI rally amid US votes
article:
(Nov 4) : Asian tech stocks looked set to rise after a revival in the artificial-intelligence trade lifted Wall Street, as investors awaited the results of the US midterm elections.

Equity-index futures for South Korea and Taiwan pointed higher, while those for Australia fell. Contracts for Japanese stocks edged lower as traders returned from a holiday.

US chipmakers rallied, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index climbing 2.6% after a recent rout fueled by concerns over the scale of AI spending. The rebound lifted the Nasdaq 100 by 0.7%. Adding to the optimism, Super Micro Computer Inc. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. both gave stronger-than-expected revenue forecasts, while Meta Platforms Inc. drew solid demand for its first bond sale in six months.

Elsewhere, Brent crude hovered near US$104 a barrel on Tuesday as traders weighed conflicting signals on US-Iran peace talks. Treasury yields rose after US job openings climbed to a four-month high, while the dollar strengthened.

The rebound in technology shares now faces the US midterm results, which may remove a key source of uncertainty and refocus investors on the outlook for AI spending and geopolitical risks heading into year-end.

“The results could act as a clearing event removing some uncertainty, though developments around the AI theme and geopolitics are the primary forces driving markets heading into the final two months of the year,” said Angelo Kourkafas at Edward Jones.

See also: AMD forecast exceeds estimates after AI chip demand soars

Millions of Americans are casting ballots Tuesday in races that will determine control of Congress as well as a range of local issues. The first polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern time.

Polymarket is pricing roughly a 95% probability of Democrats taking the House of Representatives and about a 77% chance of winning the Senate, pointing to the possibility of a sweep of both chambers.

“Tuesday’s elections could reshape the balance of power in Washington,” said Ken Mahoney at Mahoney Asset Management. “This will be good to put behind us as it has been an anticipated volatility event for quite some time.”

See also: Chip stocks rally as bonds fall on US election day

Geopolitical risks remained in focus as oil swung in choppy trading while investors parsed conflicting signals on the trajectory of peace talks between the US and Iran.

Tehran and Washington are reviewing fresh proposals from mediators aimed at resolving their differences and avoiding a return to all-out war, according to a diplomat briefed on the matter, following limited US airstrikes overnight.

Meanwhile, signs of resilience in the US labor market pushed Treasury yields higher. Job openings unexpectedly rose in September to a four-month high, while layoffs fell to their lowest level since March 2025 and quits increased.

The data may give Federal Reserve policymakers more room to focus on persistent inflation after leaving interest rates unchanged last week. The central bank raised rates in September for the first time in three years.

“For now, all signs point to a solid labor market, even if it is difficult for pockets of workers – namely those who are unemployed,” Matthew Martin, senior US economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a note.

title: AMD forecast exceeds estimates after AI chip demand soars
article:
(Nov 4) : Advanced Micro Devices Inc., a key challenger to Nvidia Corp. in artificial intelligence chips, gave a revenue forecast that exceeded analysts’ estimates, showing that demand for data center processors remains strong.

Fourth-quarter revenue will be US$17 billion, plus or minus 3%, the chipmaker said in a statement Tuesday. That easily topped the average analyst estimate of US$16.3 billion, helping send the shares up about 8% in late trading.

The outlook provided fresh evidence that AI spending is sustainable, soothing jittery investors. Shares of chipmakers and other tech companies have been battered in recent weeks over concerns about a bubble in the AI infrastructure industry.

“AMD’s earnings are simultaneously a test of its own performance and of the broader AI trade,” Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne said in a note. The results “will give investors encouragement given the recent tech and semiconductor selloff, as investors increasingly scrutinize AI spending and its returns.”

AMD’s outlook — along with a strong forecast from server maker Super Micro Computer Inc. — helped spark a late-trading rally among AI equipment makers and cloud providers. Shares of companies from CoreWeave Inc. and Nebius Group NV to Dell Technologies Inc. and Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. all gained.

Under Chief Executive Officer Lisa Su, AMD has become one of the most important suppliers of processors and computers that operate at the heart of AI facilities, underpinning a flood of new services.

See also: Chip stocks rally as bonds fall on US election day

“Our fourth-quarter outlook reflects accelerating revenue and earnings growth, driven by strong demand across our data center portfolio,” Chief Financial Officer Jean Hu said in the statement.

Even with recent market turbulence, AMD shares have more than doubled this year. The company’s valuation reached US$1 trillion in September, putting it in an elite group.

The data center growth has helped AMD offset a slump in the personal computer market, where rising memory-chip costs have slowed production and depressed user demand. Intel Corp., AMD’s top rival in that field, suffered its worst stock decline in decades after a downbeat earnings report last week.

See also: S&P 500 falls as chip rout offsets US-Iran hopes

One possible weak spot for AMD: Its gross margin will narrow to about 55% in the fourth quarter. That measure — the percentage of sales after removing production costs — had been 56% in the previous period.

AMD’s third-quarter sales rose 45% to US$13.4 billion. Profit climbed to US$2.09 a share, minus certain items. Analysts on average had predicted revenue of US$13.1 billion and earnings of US$1.97 a share.

AMD continues to deliver record results and now boasts sales that are twice as big as they were two years ago. It’s also been outperforming longtime nemesis Intel in the market for central processing units, or CPUs. But the company is still well behind Nvidia in so-called AI accelerators, which are used to train and run artificial intelligence models.

Sales at AMD’s data center business nearly doubled to US$8.5 billion. Analysts had predicted a total of US$8.2 billion. PC and gaming-related sales shrank 8% to US$3.7 billion.

Like other makers of components for PCs, AMD is suffering from a side effect of the data center boom. AI servers require a massive amount of memory. That’s cut into the supply of chips available for laptops and desktop machines — and forced prices up.

AMD is debuting new product ranges in both the CPU and accelerator markets. The Santa Clara, California-based company is also taking on Nvidia more directly with its Helios server design.

But Nvidia, the largest chipmaker and world’s most valuable company, hasn’t been standing still. It’s updating its own lineup at a fast pace and branching out into everything from software to networking to complete computers.

title: Chip stocks rally as bonds fall on US election day
article:
(Nov 4) : A revival of the artificial-intelligence trade powered Wall Street gains, bonds fell and the dollar rose on US Election Day.

Chipmakers halted a selloff that had been fueled by worries the AI spending spree is becoming harder to justify. The rebound lifted the S&P 500 even as most of its firms fell. In late hours, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Super Micro Computer Inc. gave strong forecasts. Oil prices eased. But that wasn’t enough to lift Treasuries amid solid job openings data.

Millions of Americans across the country are casting ballots in races Tuesday that will determine local issues as well as control of Congress. The first polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern time.

“Tuesday’s elections could reshape the balance of power in Washington,” said Ken Mahoney at Mahoney Asset Management. “This will be good to put behind us as it has been an anticipated volatility event for quite some time.”

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has never been lower 12 months after a midterm election, noted Tom Essaye at The Sevens Report.

“The results could act as a clearing event removing some uncertainty, though developments around the AI theme and geopolitics are the primary forces driving markets heading into the final two months of the year,” said Angelo Kourkafas at Edward Jones.

See also: S&P 500 falls as chip rout offsets US-Iran hopes

November has historically been a favorable month for equities, but the recent tech weakness has raised questions about market leadership, Mahoney noted.

At Edward Jones, Brian Therien said the recent market rotation represented less of a rejection of AI’s potential than a reassessment of the price that investors are willing to pay for it.

“Markets still assign premium valuations to companies that demonstrate strong demand, rising AI-related revenue, and the ability to fund additional investment internally,” he said. “We continue to recommend an overweight allocation to equities, with a preference for US large- and mid-cap stocks, due in part to the relative strength of the US economy.”

See also: Trump says US-Canada trade deal is close after talks with Carney

Apollo Global Management Inc. said it plans to take a more defensive approach to its investments tied to AI, as the asset manager plows billions into financing the infrastructure buildout underpinning the technology.

“We know that society will use dramatically more computing power in the future,” that demand for chips will remain strong, “and that AI capabilities are improving at an extraordinary rate,” Apollo President Jim Zelter said on a call with analysts Tuesday. “What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
